name: RNO-G

facility_roles.quote: located at 72°35'46" N, 38°25'19" W at the peak of the Greenland ice cap

intervals.label: design
intervals.quote: RNO-G will be the first production-scale radio detector for in-ice neutrino signals

intervals.label: phased construction (first two field seasons)
intervals.quote: The array is currently in phased construction near Summit Station on the Greenland ice sheet, with 7 stations deployed during the first two boreal summer field seasons of 2021 and 2022
intervals.note: 2021 season 24 May-19 Aug; 2022 season 9 May-15 Aug, per the Summit Station project page.

intervals.label: deployment paused for evaluation
intervals.quote: RNO-G paused deployment in 2023 in order to evaluate the instrument performance and design aspects before pushing forward to complete the array.
intervals.note: Status remains 'construction' (not shutdown/cancelled): the collaboration's own 2024 paper frames this as a pause before continuing, not a stop.

physics_goals.value: Detect ultra-high-energy (PeV-scale and above) astrophysical and cosmogenic neutrinos using in-ice radio detection at the top of the Greenland ice sheet
physics_goals.quote: RNO-G will be the first production-scale radio detector for in-ice neutrino signals

quantity.quote: with 7 stations deployed during the first two boreal summer field seasons of 2021 and 2022
The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) is under construction at the Summit Station in Greenland to search for ultra-high-energy neutrinos. Each of the 35 stations to be deployed
The square grid has an inter-station spacing of 1.25 km

summary.plain: A radio-antenna neutrino detector being built into the ice at the very top of Greenland's ice sheet, one station at a time, to catch the radio flash from the highest-energy neutrinos from space.
summary.technical: In-ice radio neutrino detector under phased construction at Summit Station, Greenland (72°35'46"N 38°25'19"W, atop >3 km of ice); design target 35 stations on a 1.25 km grid, each with three boreholes (~100 m deep) holding 15 receiving antennas in total plus 9 near-surface antennas. 7 stations deployed over the 2021-2022 field seasons; deployment paused in 2023 to evaluate instrument performance before continuing.
